thread.title: Apple: A Great Buy Amidst Market Fear - Apple Inc. AAPL)

author: Niki Schranz
title: Apple: A Great Buy Amidst Market Fear - Apple Inc. AAPL)
text:
Investing Thesis The market has given us a late Christmas present. Due to a "perfect" storm of negative news headlines and a falling general market, Apple ( AAPL ) shares are down considerably from their late summer highs. However, fears of stalling growth (or even a decline) are way overblown and mainly based on rumors.
Apple remains one of the (if not the) strongest businesses on the planet. They will continue to show solid EPS and modest revenue growth while returning tons of capital to shareholders. Be greedy when others are fearful. Apple shares are a buy.
Assessing The Damage Apple shares have been hit very hard during the last few months, falling more than 30% from their all-time highs. What has caused this precipitous drop? The shares actually held up pretty well in the October tech sell-off but since reporting earnings in early November have been hit by several negative headlines:
Although the company beat both revenue and EPS estimates in Q4 2018 they released soft guidance for the all-important upcoming first quarter. At the midpoint of guidance, revenue is projected to grow only 3% in Q1 2019, a serious decline from Q1 2018 where they grew revenue more than 12%. Apple decided to stop disclosing unit sales numbers going forward. Some investors took this as an attempt from management to hide a coming drop in iPhone sales. Subsequently, some suppliers started cutting their guidance, strengthening the bearish case that Q1 numbers are going to be more disappointing than projected by management. On top of that, the trade war with China created negative headlines for Apple, spreading fear that China sales will plummet. Finally, Apple shares couldn’t resist the pull from the general market drop. If you add all this up it appears that FUD is at its maximum today. But are all these concerns really warranted?
Debunking Some Of The Current Fears In my view, all of these negative news stories relating to Apple's business (maybe with a minor exception of slowing growth concerns) have not been proven by actual facts yet.
Take for example the supplier guidance cuts: I have owned Apple shares since early 2012 now and I cannot count the times I have read news stories about supply chain concerns. If there's one thing these stories have in common, other than being a waste of time to read, it's that they always seem to miss the mark. Here is a quote from Tim Cook from 2013:
I would suggest it's good to question the accuracy of any kind of rumor about build plans and also stress that even if a particular data point were factual, it would be impossible to accurately interpret the data point as to what it meant for our overall business because the supply chain is very complex. And we obviously have multiple sources for things, yields might vary, supplier performance can vary, the beginning inventory positions can vary. I mean, there's just an inordinate long list of things that would make any single data point not a great proxy for what's going on.
It's completely beyond me why analysts waste so much time trying to predict sales numbers from supplier data (which is, as Tim Cook correctly pointed out, a very limited data set) when you can see the actual numbers every three months in the earnings reports anyway. Freaking out now about possible weakness by looking at individual suppliers seems a bit senseless to me. I'm not saying there's no chance that Apple will report weak numbers in Q1 2019. All I'm saying is wait for the actual report. Then figure out what's happening. Apple is simply too big to make any meaningful conclusions from various supplier news.
The same applies to the China issue. Much ado about nothing. I think it cannot be denied that there's a business risk attached to the trade war and sentiment toward US companies in China. China sales make up almost 20% of revenues and, thus, any hiccup could have a major impact on the business and shares of Apple. However, as with the supplier guidance cuts, recent negative news regarding China and any deductions thereof is pure speculation. There is no way of telling how China sales will be in the next quarter and beyond that. Investors simply will have to wait for what transpires in the actual earnings report (which is in early February, so not very far out).
How will we evaluate China in the next report? Looking back, in Q4 2018 Greater China sales amounted to 18.1% of total revenue, basically unchanged from the previous quarter (17.9%) and Q4 2017 (18.6%). In Q1 2018 China sales amounted to 20.3% and in Q1 2017 they were at 20.7%.
If I had to make a prediction, I would say that China sales will be somewhere in that range in Q1 2019 as well. At the end of the day, Apple products have global consumer appeal because of their quality and their brand perception. Both things remain unchanged. I see no reason why a significant amount of people would let themselves be influenced by politics when purchasing electronic devices. Until proven otherwise, I would stick to this narrative.
Did Management Lose Trust? One of the biggest stories of Apple's last earnings report was their announcement to stop disclosing unit sales numbers. Many investors were very concerned. The most common fear is that iPhone sales have finally plateaued or – even worse – that management is hiding something bad. Some investors argued that the decision leads to a serious reduction of transparency and a loss of confidence in management.
Here's what management had to say about the decision in the Q4 earnings call:
When you look at our financial performance in recent years, take the last three years, for example, the number of units sold during any quarter has not been necessarily representative of the underlying strength of our business. If you look at our revenue, given the last three years, if you look at our net income during the last three years, if you look at our stock price here in the last three years, there's no correlation to the units sold in any given period.
If you look at the actual numbers of unit sales you will see that this statement is absolutely true:
( Source: Author; Earnings Reports Q1/2015 - Q4/2018)
As you can see unit sales have been pretty stable over the last four years. If you assumed that unit sales numbers were predictive of business strength you would have looked at this picture and concluded that business must have been flat for years. But now look at this:
AAPL data by YCharts
Revenue has been up, EPS has been up even more and also the share price – despite the recent fall – has performed well. Looking at these graphs, it becomes clear that management is absolutely right in their assessment. Unit sales do not correlate with business strength.
However, if you have followed Apple in the last few years – and the news in the last two months – you will be aware of the fact that unit sales numbers, actually iPhone sales numbers, were a very important metric many investors and analysts were looking at to evaluate Apple's business strength. That is somewhat understandable because iPhone sales make up the majority of revenues and profits and investors were obviously trying to evaluate the health of the business from as many angles as possible. Unit sales seemed to be a very pure metric, painting a very clear picture of the commercial success of the all-important iPhone.
The problem is, though, that this sometimes excessive focus on unit sales numbers created a lot of negative noise in the past. That's very problematic for shareholders since we just saw that unit sales numbers were basically flat and didn't have any predictive value for the business in the last years.
Apple is actively changing the narrative away from iPhone units, and by doing so, they are removing a major distraction to shareholders, which is a good thing, in my opinion. In that vein, the company also announced that it will start breaking out the other products category to wearables, home, and accessories as well as reporting the gross margins of the services segment.
In other words, the company is removing transparency where it is of no value to shareholders (unit sales) and adding transparency where shareholders have a very high interest in (services, other products) because they are the major future growth drivers.
Besides that, Apple will continue to disclose the dollar amounts for iPhone sales, which arguably was the much more meaningful metric anyways. So fears of lack of transparency or that management wants to hide something turn out to be completely unfounded. Apple's management has a long history of being transparent and trustworthy. That hasn't changed in my view with this change in reporting.
Is The Market Onto Something? Why, therefore, are some investors afraid that the company will miss big in Q1 2019, contrary to management guidance? To be honest, I have no idea. Apple has been very consistent in meeting or exceeding expectations in the past. There's no substantiated reason to believe that the company will start missing their own guidance now. As I've already said, most current fears are founded on rumors or "analysis" based on limited and unreliable data sets. If history is any guide, management should be able to meet or even exceed projections.
If you take a look back at the chart above you will notice that the share price seems to be highly correlated with the growth of revenues and to an even greater extent EPS. That makes sense since Apple is a very mature company where EPS should naturally be the No. 1 metric to follow. However, with the recent share price drop, the correlation between EPS/revenue and share price appears to be broken. You could, therefore, conclude that the market is forecasting a decline in EPS and revenues as has been the case in 2015/2016.
Could it be that the market knows something that we don't?
I believe the stock market is a tremendous machine for processing information that can give valuable insights about a business' performance. I would never bluntly disregard the information given by the market, which is, in Apple's case, "something is wrong." However, as I try to argue in this article, I think shares are down because of a perfect storm of bad news, rumors, wrong interpretation of facts and general market turmoil. Maybe shares deserved a little pullback because of slowing growth. Did it justify a 30%-plus haircut in share price? I think not.
Also, if you look at the reported and projected numbers you cannot really make a case for a decline in EPS. In the last quarter, the company reported astounding EPS growth of 41%. Analysts are projecting EPS for Q1 2019 in the range of 4.41 to 4.85 and a midpoint of 4.66, which would translate to almost 20% growth, up from 16% growth in Q1 2018 – that means EPS growth is actually accelerating in the next quarter. TTM EPS would come in at 12.64 in Q1 2019, and, thus, continuing the upward trend of the EPS-line in the graph above.
According to Nasdaq.com , analysts are expecting EPS of 13.18 in 2019 and 14.7 in 2020 at the midpoint. That would translate to yoy-growth of 12% and 10%, respectively, which is considerably down from the 29% EPS growth rate in 2018 but still projecting double-digit growth in the coming two years.
Identifying Main Catalysts For Shares In my view, there are three main catalysts that should propel shares higher in the near, mid and long term:
Removal of FUD with next earnings report (Q1 2019). Next iPhone supercycle with 5G implementation within the next two years . Long-term growth of other products and especially the services segment. I've already spoken to the first point. I think it's very likely that management will positively surprise Wall Street considerably in the next earnings report. This alone should be a big boost to shares in the near term.
Regarding the second point, I think it's self evident that the change to 5G will incentivize many Apple users to upgrade their iPhones since the new technology will not be available for old devices. It's unclear yet when Apple will release their first 5G iPhone and it's also unclear when 5G technology will reach the kind of mass adoption that will make it indispensable for consumers. However, for long-term investors, the change to 5G is a clear catalyst for Apple's business and definitely something to watch out for in the next 2-3 years.
Turning to the last point, the growth of services and other products, this is really the main storyline for Apple going forward, in my opinion. Apple has been trying to emphasize the importance of these segments (especially the services segment) for some time now. However, given the importance and continued success of iPhone sales (they still accounted for 60% of revenues in the most recent quarter) many investors haven't really bought into that story yet. Be that as it may, it's undeniable that services are becoming an increasingly important part of Apple's business:
( Source: Author; Earnings Reports Q1/2015 - Q4/2018)
As you can see the services segment has steadily outgrown total sales and as of now represents 14% of total revenue. More importantly, services revenue growth has actually accelerated in 2018, which shows the strength of this business segment. Furthermore, services should have higher margins than the overall business and, thus, drive profitability even more than revenues. We will see the actual margin numbers next quarter.
Also encouraging for the growth thesis in services is that the installed base for Apple products is still rising. For example, JPMorgan expects the iPhone installed base to increase between 7% to 8% in the next three years. This should create nice tailwinds for the services and the overall business of Apple (and, by the way, flies in the face of many investors painting a doomsday scenario for shares).
You could easily write an article alone about the developments and opportunities in the services segment. To cut it short: App Store, Apple Pay, cloud services, Apple Music and especially healthcare are massive long-term business opportunities. There's no evidence to my knowledge that services growth will slow down any time soon. On the contrary, I think it's quite likely that services revenue will grow above 20% for many years to come. If you couple that with increased revenues from other products and stable core-product sales, business should do very well going forward.
Concluding thoughts After taking a hard look, I think it's quite clear that Apple shares are surrounded by a lot of unreasonable FUD at the moment. I simply couldn't identify any convincing evidence that would confirm the current level of FUD and justify the sharp share price drop. Concerns about slowing growth are somewhat warranted. But who really thought that Apple will grow revenues consistently above 10%-15% at their size? What matters more, in my opinion, is EPS growth. And there are no signs of a slowdown in that regard – actually analysts predict that yoy EPS growth will accelerate in Q1 2019.
iPhone sale decline worries and concerns about the unforgiving law of large numbers have created a problematic narrative for Apple shares. Basically, it tells us that Apple’s days as an innovative growth company are over. After all, Apple already is the most profitable company on the planet by far. They own most profits in a saturated smartphone market, which still accounts for the lion's share of the company's revenues and profits. Even worse, the company will stop disclosing unit sales numbers, seemingly confirming the hunch that something fundamental is going wrong. Thus, reads the conclusion of this narrative, Apple has only one way to go from here: Down.
There's some truth to this sentiment. As an investor, you can't expect similar growth rates and investment returns from Apple shares as we have seen in the past when Apple was a much smaller company. That's simply impossible. But does that mean that the businesses decline is imminent? Well, you know the old expression: Nope .
The last time I heard comparable concerns from investors about Apple's upcoming business decline was in 2015/2016. And while revenues and EPS actually declined in 2016, looking back, that drop appears to have been merely a blip on the radar. Revenue is up 23% and EPS is up 43% since then.
Apple has shown a remarkable ability to grow it's business consistently even at the large scale it's operating today. At the same time, they are a great example of balancing growth, profitability, and return of capital to shareholders . At current prices, their dividend yield stands at almost 1.9%, their payout ratio is roughly 25% and dividend growth has been accelerating from 9.6% in 2016 to 10.5% in 2017 and 15.9% in 2018. The company is trading at a TTM PE of 13.16 and a forward PE of 11.8. Their forward PEG ratio is 0.45. This seems way too cheap for a quality company like Apple.
My perception is that most of the bad news surrounding Apple already is priced in the shares. Therefore, shareholders find themselves in a pretty comfortable position: If the company actually disappoints in Q1 2019, the downside risk is limited because of the already low expectations. However, If negativity doesn’t materialize to the extent projected or if the company can surprise positively, shares have significant upside potential. Regardless of short-term considerations, shares remain a solid long-term holding and a great buy at current levels.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL.
